report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < .01", "p > .04", "p < .01", 
"p-value <.01", "p ≤ .01", "p < .01"), Text = c("These failures were surprising because the original study produced a p < .01 while the replication yielded a significant effect in the opposite direction.", 
"Only 2 of 11 studies (18%) reporting p > .04 replicated, compared with 20 of 32 (63%) studies reporting p < .001.", 
"I reviewed replications of six studies where an original claim statistic had p < .01, but the replication produced a significant reverse effect.", 
"The SCORE dataset contained 15 claims where the original study produced a p-value <.01 but the replication found a significant effect in a different pattern.", 
"Two of these four also reported p ≤ .01, but the replication did not produce a significant effect in either direction.", 
"The most notable replication failure was the original study's claim that scores on the TAS-20's \"difficulty to identify feelings\" (DIF) subscale positively correlated with recognition accuracy for joy words in the happy music condition (r partial = .343, p < .01)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > .04 ", "p = .149", "p = .48"), Sentence = c("Only 2 of 11 studies (18%) reporting p > .04 replicated, compared with 20 of 32 (63%) studies reporting p < .001.", "Pairwise comparisons of the correct estimates from the replicator's models revealed that Spanish ELLs had significantly lower initial proficiency than Asian ELLs and English native speakers (Spanish ELLs: 63.1, Asian ELLs: 75.4, native speakers: 68.7; ps < .001) 2 . this analysis did not replicate Roberts et al.'s slope difference (Spanish: 22.7 vs Asian: 23.6; p = .149), the direction was no longer reversed, a marked difference from the conclusions of the two SCORE replications.", "In contrast, the replication data showed a positive correlation for the BPAS (r = .65, p < .001) and no significant correlation for the AAQ (r = .09, p = .48)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 4 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (4). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. info.title: Underestimating the replicability of the social and behavioural sciences: an audit of six surprising SCORE replication failures

text.text: The Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) project recently published a large-scale replication project within the social and behavioural sciences 1 .
The authors replicated only 151 of 274 (55%) claims, a finding covered by major outlets such as the New York Times 2 and Forbes 3 .
Here, I audited SCORE replications of six studies where at least one claim surprisingly failed to replicate.
These failures were surprising because the original study produced a p < .01 while the replication yielded a significant effect in the opposite direction.
text.formatted: These failures were surprising because the original study produced a p < .01 while the replication yielded a significant effect in the opposite direction.

text.text: I show that, of the 12 claims tested across these six replications, five were miscategorised as failed replications because of data analysis and interpretation problems, and six replications were invalid because of poor data quality and an error in the replication's experiment code.

I conclude that individual replications within replicability projects may benefit from more thorough peer review, and that a more comprehensive audit is necessary before we can be confident in the project's overall replicability estimate.
The replication crisis is often attributed to underpowered studies and flexible analyses producing false positives and inflated effect-size estimates [4] [5] [6] .
text.formatted: The replication crisis is often attributed to underpowered studies and flexible analyses producing false positives and inflated effect-size estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> .

text.text: This account has shaped proposed measures to improve replicability, such as preregistration and power calculations, as well as the statistical tools used to estimate replicability.

For instance, the p-curve method assesses the evidentiary value of a set of findings by testing for skew in the distribution of significant p-values 7 , while the z-curve uses significant p-values to estimate the average power of a set of tests 8 .

These methods work because the distribution of significant p-values depends on statistical power: high-powered studies are more likely to produce very small p-values, and true null effects yield uniformly distributed p-values.
We can therefore treat a body of work full of very small p-values as evidence of real, replicable effects.
This association between p-values and replicability also tells us what failed replications should look like.
Original studies with p-values just under .05 should be the least likely to replicate, and their replications should generally produce smaller or null effect size estimates.
The
Open Science Collaboration's (OSC) 9 large-scale effort to estimate the replicability of the psychological sciences found exactly this pattern.
text.formatted: Open Science Collaboration's (OSC) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> large-scale effort to estimate the replicability of the psychological sciences found exactly this pattern.

text.text: Only 2 of 11 studies (18%) reporting p > .04 replicated, compared with 20 of 32 (63%) studies reporting p < .001.
text.formatted: Only 2 of 11 studies (18%) reporting p > .04 replicated, compared with 20 of 32 (63%) studies reporting p < .001.

text.text: Given this pattern, it is somewhat surprising when an original study with a small p-value fails to replicate.
Especially if the replication produces a significant effect in the opposite direction.
Compared to typical replication failures, such results are more likely to reflect meaningful methodological or analytical differences between the original and replication studies.
Therefore, it is worth investigating further when two high-powered studies produce incompatible results before simply concluding that the original finding is not replicable.
Large-scale replication efforts do not usually lend themselves to this kind of investigation.
In SCORE's replication project, study protocols underwent peer review before data collection, but completed reports were reviewed only by other team members.
In other words, the reviewers may have been less familiar with the study's methods and analyses than we would expect from external reviewers invited for their expertise.
Additionally, replication reports usually lacked details, such as descriptive statistics and plots, that one would expect in an independently submitted manuscript.
Without these details, data anomalies that could explain conflicting results may be more likely to go undetected by both authors and reviewers.
In this audit, I illustrate the value of a more thorough review process by identifying methodological and analytical details that help explain some of SCORE's more surprising replication failures.
I reviewed replications of six studies where an original claim statistic had p < .01, but the replication produced a significant reverse effect.
text.formatted: I reviewed replications of six studies where an original claim statistic had p < .01, but the replication produced a significant reverse effect.

text.text: This revealed five claims that were incorrectly classified as replication failures.
For the first claim (Supplemental Materials B1), re-running the replicator's analysis script failed to reproduce their reported numbers.
Instead, the effect was significant in the same direction as in the original study.
The cause was a bug in the R package the replicators used 10 , which was not fixed until the following year.
text.formatted: The cause was a bug in the R package the replicators used <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> , which was not fixed until the following year.

text.text: Other issues stemmed from the replicators' code.
Replications of two studies, each contributing one claim, produced reverse effects because the replicators' analysis deviated from the original study.
In one case, the replicators' model included a term that was not in the original study (Supplemental Materials B3); in the other, they omitted a model term that was (Supplemental Materials B6).
Correcting these deviations yielded significant effects consistent with the original studies.
One original study contributed three claims (Supplemental Materials B2).
For two of these claims, the replicator reported the wrong model parameters.
The correct parameters supported the original finding.
The third claim was subject to replication by two independent replicators.
I found that one incorrectly filtered participants, and one omitted a model term.
Correcting these did not turn the result into a successful replication, but it shifted the result from a significant reverse effect to a non-significant effect in the same direction as the original.
Finally, reverse correlations across two online replications were traceable to poor data quality.
In one case, the replication found a positive relationship between responses on two scales whereas the original found a negative one (Supplemental Materials B4).
The original data were also available, so I could compare response distributions across the two studies.
Strikingly, responses on the psychopathology scale were positively skewed in the original, but roughly uniformly distributed in the replication.
The scales used to test the claim had no reverse-keyed items, but both studies administered two additional scales that did.
In the original dataset, responses to forward-and reverse-keyed items were negatively correlated in both scales, as expected for genuine responses.
In the replication, however, there was a positive correlation in one scale, and no significant correlation in the other.
In other words, the replication seems to have found a spurious positive correlation for the focal claim because participants responded similarly to every item across both scales.
In the second case (Supplemental Materials B5), the original study reported a positive correlation between responses on an alexithymia scale and performance on a memory task.
The replication found a negative correlation.
Average alexithymia levels were notably higher in the replication, and responses to forward-and reverse-keyed scale items were positively related, indicative of careless responding.
Performance on the memory task was similarly poor, with 30% of participants performing at or below chance.
The negative correlation between these two measures therefore appears to be an artefact of careless responses, which simultaneously inflated alexithymia scores and reduced memory task accuracy.
This replication also contributed four more failed tests (albeit not as surprising) to SCORE's dataset.

Another major error meant that the replication would have been invalid even without data quality issues; an inspection of the online materials revealed that the experiment played the wrong music prime in one condition, meaning one of its focal manipulations was not implemented correctly.
What can we conclude from such a small audit of replication failures?
Because I selected claims based on their p-values, the percentage of false negatives observed here is almost certainly much higher than in SCORE's full dataset.
But that does not mean there are not a meaningful number of problematic replications still to be identified.
Even among the 15 replication failures I identified as surprising, I only briefly audited eight claims.
Moreover, I did not examine other categories of surprising findings.
Cases where the original effect was highly significant and produced a near-zero or reversed (but not significant) effect also warrant further investigation.
Finally, because I only examined replication failures, this audit could not identify failed replications misclassified as successes.
In sum, much more work is needed before we can judge whether, and to what extent, SCORE's overall replicability estimate requires revision.
What we can conclude is that SCORE's quality control efforts were insufficient to prevent a non-trivial number of false negatives (and perhaps even false positives) in their dataset.
This audit was post hoc and driven by priors about the replicability of original findings with small p-values.
As research shows, prior beliefs can bias how researchers analyse and interpret data 11 .
text.formatted: As research shows, prior beliefs can bias how researchers analyse and interpret data <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: But in some cases, such priors can help detect a study's shortcomings.
A famous example in psychology is Bem's 12 experiments on extrasensory perception.
text.formatted: A famous example in psychology is Bem's <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> experiments on extrasensory perception.

text.text: Priors about the laws of nature drove scrutiny of the project, which helped reveal that common statistical practices in the psychological sciences were conducive to false positives 4, 13 .
text.formatted: Priors about the laws of nature drove scrutiny of the project, which helped reveal that common statistical practices in the psychological sciences were conducive to false positives <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: Considering the plausibility of results and data distributions could have strengthened SCORE's quality control process.

For example, one of the claims audited here was a quite plausible finding that Spanish English language learners had lower reading achievement than native English speakers at the beginning of the study 14 .
text.formatted: For example, one of the claims audited here was a quite plausible finding that Spanish English language learners had lower reading achievement than native English speakers at the beginning of the study <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: A replication study finding the opposite would ideally prompt, at the very least, a closer look at the methods and analyses.
It is critical to distinguish clearly between auditing failed replications and post-hoc rationalisation 15 .
text.formatted: It is critical to distinguish clearly between auditing failed replications and post-hoc rationalisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Although I selected replications to examine based on their results, the problems I identified would require correction regardless of their conclusions.
The impact of any issues discovered in a review must be demonstrated.

For instance, it is not enough to argue that a replication is invalid because of a single unusual descriptive statistic, such as a high average on a particular measure, without showing how this would explain the observed results.
Finally, audits should avoid post-hoc theorising based on differences between original and replication studies 15.
text.formatted: Finally, audits should avoid post-hoc theorising based on differences between original and replication studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref>.

text.text: Many effects in the social and behavioural sciences may be context-or demographic-sensitive 16 , and a replication may indeed fail because of a previously undiscovered moderator, but such moderation should be demonstrated in new data before being proposed as an explanation.
text.formatted: Many effects in the social and behavioural sciences may be context-or demographic-sensitive <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> , and a replication may indeed fail because of a previously undiscovered moderator, but such moderation should be demonstrated in new data before being proposed as an explanation.

text.text: Whether the kinds of issues identified here are more likely in large-scale replication projects than in individually submitted papers cannot be answered by an audit.
Nevertheless, it is easy to imagine how conventional peer review of a full manuscript with descriptive statistics and plots could have identified and prevented several of the problems seen here.
For example, a reviewer familiar with psychopathology symptoms would likely suspect that something is amiss upon seeing a uniform distribution of scores on a psychopathology scale.

It is possible that SCORE's overall replicability estimate is nevertheless accurate because the issues identified here occurred very rarely, or because they produced false positives and false negatives at similar rates.
But the project's results also speak to the replicability of individual claims.
For this reason, a comprehensive, systematic audit may be warranted, perhaps starting with the most surprising findings.
Fortunately, SCORE's outstanding transparency and thorough documentation make such an undertaking possible.
The audit could also collect data on how and when errors occurred to help design preventive measures for future projects.
For example, errors may be more likely when the original authors' analysis scripts are unavailable or when replicators have less familiarity with the original study's methods.
Large-scale replicability projects remain essential to documenting and improving the credibility of studies in the social and behavioural sciences.
Their impact, however, makes ensuring the reliability of their own findings all the more critical.
Implementing expert peer review of more comprehensive reports and applying greater scrutiny to implausible or surprising results would be valuable initial steps.

Without ensuring the integrity of individual replication studies, projects like SCORE risk conflating estimates of replicability with estimates of social and behavioural scientists' ability to conduct replications.
The SCORE dataset contained 15 claims where the original study produced a p-value <.01 but the replication found a significant effect in a different pattern.
text.formatted: The SCORE dataset contained 15 claims where the original study produced a p-value <.01 but the replication found a significant effect in a different pattern.

text.text: I selected eight of these claims spanning six articles to audit for potential methodological deviations or analytical errors that could explain such discrepancies.
I hand-picked these based on how straightforward the audit would be given the topic, analyses used, and my experience with both.
For example, I skipped one claim based on stock exchange data from an online platform.
Because I was unfamiliar with the platform or this kind of analysis, I did not audit its failed replication.
I did not judge whether the original study's analyses appropriately answered its research question.
In some cases, replicators may have deviated from the original study in a way that produced a more meaningful or informative result.

Because the goal was to investigate replicability, not robustness (i.e., whether the results hold under alternative model specifications), I assessed only whether the original claim was supported after running the original authors' analyses as faithfully as possible on the new data.
These were preliminary audits targeting major, visible issues, and subject-matter experts may find additional errors in more thorough investigations.
The numbers presented here should therefore be treated as illustrative rather than a corrected, final replication outcome.

I used Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 large language models (LLMs) to accelerate several aspects of the audit: screening articles for audit feasibility, finding relevant repositories, understanding their contents, locating relevant code, converting code to R when necessary, and verifying correct implementation.

text.text: The general finding was that poor economic performance is associated with more negative framing of the EU.

The SCORE project attempted to replicate Teney's claim that higher national unemployment rates are related to less cosmopolitan framing (B = -0.0034, p = .001), but found the opposite (B = 0.002, p = .046).

This may be unclear from the original paper's wording, which states that "only the significant effects of the squared terms are shown (emphasis mine)", but the original paper's associated figure confirms this, showing a linear relationship 5.
